item.question: Mowgli's friends live along the trail on the marked places below. Which of his friends will he be able to visit, if he jumps by 2 steps starting from 0?
steps_tex: Jumps of $2$ from $0$ land on $2$, $4$, $6$, $8$ and so on: the even numbers, the multiples of $2$.
The friends live at these places: ant $4$, spider $9$, frog $12$, bird $14$, Kaa $21$, Sher Khan $25$, Baloo $30$, Akela $35$, deer $39$, rabbit $50$, monkey $57$.
$4 = 2 \times 2$, $12 = 2 \times 6$, $14 = 2 \times 7$, $30 = 2 \times 15$ and $50 = 2 \times 25$, so a jump of $2$ lands on all five of these places.
$9$, $21$, $25$, $35$, $39$ and $57$ are odd numbers, so jumps of $2$ skip them.
Mowgli can visit the ant, the frog, the bird, Baloo and the rabbit. $2$ is a common factor of $4$, $12$, $14$, $30$ and $50$.
Check: $30 \div 2 = 15$ and $50 \div 2 = 25$, both exact.
item.answer_tex: The ant $(4)$, frog $(12)$, bird $(14)$, Baloo $(30)$ and rabbit $(50)$: $2$ is a common factor of $4$, $12$, $14$, $30$ and $50$.

item.question: Let us find some common factors of the numbers 24 and 36. Note that all jumps in the following questions start from 0. (a): Can we jump by 2 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36? Yes/No. 2 is/is not a common factor of 24 and 36. (b): Can we jump by 3 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36? Yes/No. 3 is/is not a common factor of 24 and 36. (c): Can we jump by 4 steps at a time to reach both 24 and 36? Yes/No. 4 is/is not a common factor of 24 and 36. (d): What other jumps can we take to reach both 24 and 36? (e): How many common factors can you find for 24 and 36? List them. (f): What about jumping by 1 step each time to reach both 24 and 36?
steps_tex: $(a)$: $2 \times 12 = 24$ and $2 \times 18 = 36$, so jumps of $2$ reach both. Yes, $2$ is a common factor of $24$ and $36$.
$(b)$: $3 \times 8 = 24$ and $3 \times 12 = 36$, so jumps of $3$ reach both. Yes, $3$ is a common factor.
$(c)$: $4 \times 6 = 24$ and $4 \times 9 = 36$, so jumps of $4$ reach both. Yes, $4$ is a common factor.

$(d)$: jumps of $6$ reach both, because $6 \times 4 = 24$ and $6 \times 6 = 36$, and so do jumps of $12$, because $12 \times 2 = 24$ and $12 \times 3 = 36$. Jumps of $8$ reach $24$ but not $36$, and jumps of $9$ reach $36$ but not $24$. The other jumps are $1$, $6$ and $12$.
$(f)$: a jump of $1$ lands on every number: $1 \times 24 = 24$ and $1 \times 36 = 36$. Yes, $1$ is a common factor of $24$ and $36$.
Check: $12 \times 2 = 24$ and $12 \times 3 = 36$, so $12$, the biggest common factor, reaches both.
steps: (a): 2 × 12 = 24 and 2 × 18 = 36, so jumps of 2 reach both. Yes, 2 is a common factor of 24 and 36.
(b): 3 × 8 = 24 and 3 × 12 = 36, so jumps of 3 reach both. Yes, 3 is a common factor.
(c): 4 × 6 = 24 and 4 × 9 = 36, so jumps of 4 reach both. Yes, 4 is a common factor.

(d): jumps of 6 reach both, because 6 × 4 = 24 and 6 × 6 = 36, and so do jumps of 12, because 12 × 2 = 24 and 12 × 3 = 36. Jumps of 8 reach 24 but not 36, and jumps of 9 reach 36 but not 24. The other jumps are 1, 6 and 12.
(e): the factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. In both lists: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. That is 6 common factors.
(f): a jump of 1 lands on every number: 1 × 24 = 24 and 1 × 36 = 36. Yes, 1 is a common factor of 24 and 36.
Check: 12 × 2 = 24 and 12 × 3 = 36, so 12, the biggest common factor, reaches both.
item.answer: (a): Yes; (b): Yes; (c): Yes; (d): 1, 6 and 12; (e): 6 common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12; (f): Yes, 1 is a common factor.

item.question: Find which of the following numbers can be reached by jumps of 4 steps? 4 is the common factor of the numbers ___.
steps_tex: $10$ is not a multiple of $4$: $4 \times 2 = 8$ and $4 \times 3 = 12$, so the jumps go from $8$ to $12$ and skip $10$.
$16 = 4 \times 4$, so a jump of $4$ reaches $16$.
$27$ is not a multiple of $4$: $4 \times 6 = 24$ and $4 \times 7 = 28$, so $27$ is skipped.
$36 = 4 \times 9$ and $48 = 4 \times 12$, so both can be reached. $0$ is the starting place.
Check: $16 \div 4 = 4$, $36 \div 4 = 9$ and $48 \div 4 = 12$, all exact.
item.answer_tex: $16$, $36$ and $48$ can be reached. $4$ is a common factor of $16$, $36$ and $48$.

item.question: Check two statements. (1) Every multiple of 4 is also a multiple of 2. (2) Every multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 4.
steps: (1): write some multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Each one is also a multiple of 2: 2 × 2 = 4, 2 × 4 = 8, 2 × 6 = 12, 2 × 8 = 16 and 2 × 10 = 20.
Why it always works: 4 = 2 × 2, so every multiple of 4 is made of 2s. Statement (1) is true.
(2): write some multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. 12 and 24 are multiples of 4, because 4 × 3 = 12 and 4 × 6 = 24, but 6 is not: 4 × 1 = 4 and 4 × 2 = 8.
One multiple of 6 that is not a multiple of 4 is enough. 6 is one, so statement (2) is false.
Check: 18 is another example. 4 × 4 = 16 and 4 × 5 = 20, so 18 is not a multiple of 4.
item.answer: (1) is true because 4 = 2 × 2. (2) is false: 6 is a multiple of 6 but not of 4

item.question: Sort the numbers 16, 35, 60, 48, 85 and 70 into: divisible by 2 only, divisible by 5 only, and divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
steps: 16: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 exactly. 5 × 3 = 15 and 5 × 4 = 20, so 16 is not divisible by 5. 16 is divisible by 2 only.
35: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 exactly. 2 × 17 = 34 and 2 × 18 = 36, so 35 is not divisible by 2. 35 is divisible by 5 only.
60: 60 ÷ 2 = 30, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 and 60 ÷ 10 = 6, all exact. 60 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
48: 48 ÷ 2 = 24 exactly. 5 × 9 = 45 and 5 × 10 = 50, so 48 is not divisible by 5. 48 is divisible by 2 only.
85: 85 ÷ 5 = 17 exactly. 2 × 42 = 84 and 2 × 43 = 86, so 85 is not divisible by 2. 85 is divisible by 5 only.
70: 70 ÷ 2 = 35, 70 ÷ 5 = 14 and 70 ÷ 10 = 7, all exact. 70 is divisible by 2, 5 and 10.
No number is divisible by 10 only: 60 and 70 are divisible by 10, and both are also divisible by 2 and 5.
item.answer: 2 only: 16 and 48. 5 only: 35 and 85. 2, 5 and 10: 60 and 70. None is divisible by 10 only

item.question: State whether the following statements are true (T) or false (F). (a): Factors of even numbers must be even. (b): Multiples of odd numbers cannot be even. (c): Factors of odd numbers cannot be even. (d): One of the common multiples of two consecutive numbers is their product. (e): The only common factor of any two consecutive numbers is 1. (f): 0 cannot be a factor of any number.
steps_tex: $(a)$: False. $12$ is even, and $3$ is a factor of $12$, because $3 \times 4 = 12$, but $3$ is odd. $1$ is also an odd factor of every even number.
$(b)$: False. $3$ is odd, and $3 \times 2 = 6$ is a multiple of $3$ that is even.

$(c)$: True. If an even number were a factor of an odd number, the odd number would be a multiple of an even number, and every multiple of an even number is even. The factors of $15$ are $1$, $3$, $5$, $15$ and of $21$ are $1$, $3$, $7$, $21$: all odd.

$(d)$: True. Take $4$ and $5$: $4 \times 5 = 20$, and $20$ is a multiple of $4$ and of $5$. Take $8$ and $9$: $8 \times 9 = 72$, a multiple of both. A product is always a multiple of the numbers multiplied.

$(e)$: True. The factors of $8$ are $1$, $2$, $4$, $8$ and of $9$ are $1$, $3$, $9$: only $1$ is common. The factors of $14$ are $1$, $2$, $7$, $14$ and of $15$ are $1$, $3$, $5$, $15$: only $1$ is common. A jump bigger than $1$ lands on a number and then at least $2$ steps further, so it cannot land on both a number and the next number.
$(f)$: True. A jump of $0$ steps stays at $0$ for ever, so it can never reach a number. $0 \times$ any number is $0$, so $0$ only makes the number $0$.
Check: $12 \div 3 = 4$, so $3$ does divide $12$, and $3 \times 2 = 6$ is even.
item.answer_tex: $(a)$: False; $(b)$: False; $(c)$: True; $(d)$: True; $(e)$: True; $(f)$: True
steps: (a): False. 12 is even, and 3 is a factor of 12, because 3 × 4 = 12, but 3 is odd. 1 is also an odd factor of every even number.
(b): False. 3 is odd, and 3 × 2 = 6 is a multiple of 3 that is even.

(c): True. If an even number were a factor of an odd number, the odd number would be a multiple of an even number, and every multiple of an even number is even. The factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5, 15 and of 21 are 1, 3, 7, 21: all odd.
(d): True. Take 4 and 5: 4 × 5 = 20, and 20 is a multiple of 4 and of 5. Take 8 and 9: 8 × 9 = 72, a multiple of both. A product is always a multiple of the numbers multiplied.

(e): True. The factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8 and of 9 are 1, 3, 9: only 1 is common. The factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7, 14 and of 15 are 1, 3, 5, 15: only 1 is common. A jump bigger than 1 lands on a number and then at least 2 steps further, so it cannot land on both a number and the next number.
(f): True. A jump of 0 steps stays at 0 for ever, so it can never reach a number. 0 × any number is 0, so 0 only makes the number 0.
Check: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 3 does divide 12, and 3 × 2 = 6 is even.

steps_tex: Count the day they start together as day $0$, like the start of a number line.
Sher Khan hunts on days $3$, $6$, $9$, $12$, $15$, $18$, $21$, $24$, $27$, $30$, and so on: the multiples of $3$.
Bagheera hunts on days $5$, $10$, $15$, $20$, $25$, $30$, and so on: the multiples of $5$.
Both hunt on days $15$, $30$, $45$ and so on. These are the common multiples of $3$ and $5$, and the first is day $15$, because $3 \times 5 = 15$.
Check: $3 \times 10 = 30$ and $5 \times 6 = 30$; $3 \times 15 = 45$ and $5 \times 9 = 45$.

Mowgli wants to meet his friend Baloo the bear but wants to avoid Sher Khan's house. How long (in steps) could each jump be? steps_tex: $(a)$: a jump meets Baloo at $30$ when the jump size is a factor of $30$. The factors of $30$ are $1$, $2$, $3$, $5$, $6$, $10$, $15$, $30$.
A jump avoids Sher Khan at $25$ when the jump size is not a factor of $25$. The factors of $25$ are $1$, $5$, $25$.
Take out the jump sizes that land on $25$: $1$, because $1 \times 25 = 25$, and $5$, because $5 \times 5 = 25$.
The jumps that meet Baloo and avoid Sher Khan are $2$, $3$, $6$, $10$, $15$ and $30$ steps.
$(b)$: the jump must be a common factor of $21$ and $35$. The factors of $21$ are $1$, $3$, $7$, $21$ and of $35$ are $1$, $5$, $7$, $35$. Common: $1$ and $7$.
Check: $7 \times 3 = 21$ and $7 \times 5 = 35$. Also $6 \times 5 = 30$, and jumps of $6$ go $24$ then $30$, skipping $25$.

The jumps that meet Baloo and avoid Sher Khan are 2, 3, 6, 10, 15 and 30 steps.

item.question: Sort the following numbers into those that are (a): divisible by 2 only (b): divisible by 5 only (c): divisible by 10 only (d): divisible by 2, 5, and 10. 90, 22, 38, 30, 75, 45, 66, 78, 62, 40, 84, 56, 25, 95, 55
steps_tex: A number is divisible by $2$ when $2$ is a factor of it. The same is true for $5$ and for $10$.
$90$: $90 \div 2 = 45$, $90 \div 5 = 18$ and $90 \div 10 = 9$, all exact. $90$ is divisible by $2$, $5$ and $10$.

$22$, $38$, $66$, $78$, $62$, $84$ and $56$ are divisible by $2$ but not by $5$ (for example $22 \div 2 = 11$, but $5 \times 4 = 20$ and $5 \times 5 = 25$ skip $22$). So these $7$ are divisible by $2$ only.
$75$, $45$, $25$, $95$ and $55$ are divisible by $5$ but not by $2$, because they are odd (for example $45 \div 5 = 9$). So these $5$ are divisible by $5$ only.
No number is divisible by $10$ only: a number divisible by $10$ is also divisible by $2$ and $5 (10 = 2 \times 5)$, so $90$, $30$ and $40$ go in the middle.
Check: $7 + 5 + 3 = 15$, the same as the number of cards.
